Question:
Let \(\{a_k\}_{k=1}^{2011}\) be the sequence of real numbers defined by \(a_1 = 0.201,\) \(a_2 = (0.2011)^{a_1},\) \(a_3 = (0.20101)^{a_2},\) and \(a_4 = (0.201011)^{a_3},\) and more generally \[ a_k = \begin{cases} \tiny \left(0.\underbrace{20101\ldots0101}_{k+2 \text{ digits}}\right)^{a_{k-1}}, & \tiny \text{if } k \text{ is odd,} \\ \tiny \left(0.\underbrace{20101\ldots01011}_{k+2 \text{ digits}}\right)^{a_{k-1}}, & \tiny \text{if } k \text{ is even.} \end{cases} \]

Rearranging the numbers in the sequence \(\{a_k\}_{k=1}^{2011}\) in decreasing order produces a new sequence \(\{b_k\}_{k=1}^{2011}.\) What is the sum of all the integers \(k,\) \(1 \le k \le 2011,\) such that \(a_k = b_k?\)
Solution:
Let \(c_k\) denote the decimal base used to define \(a_k\), with \(c_1=0.201\). Comparing their digits shows that the odd-indexed bases increase, the even-indexed bases decrease, and every odd-indexed base is below every even-indexed base. For example,
\[
c_1<c_3<c_5<c_6<c_4<c_2.
\]
These comparisons suggest that the terms themselves may form two interlacing lists, but the exponents must also be checked.

For \(0<c<1\), the value \(c^t\) decreases as \(t\) increases. For a fixed positive exponent, it increases as the positive base increases. We will use both facts together.

Introduce \(a_0=1\), so that \(a_1=c_1^{a_0}\) and the recurrence \(a_k=c_k^{a_{k-1}}\) works from \(k=1\). All terms \(a_k\) for \(k\ge1\) lie strictly between \(0\) and \(1\). Also,
\[
a_1<c_2<a_2<a_0,
\]
because \(a_1<1\) and raising \(c_2\in(0,1)\) to an exponent below \(1\) increases its value.

We now prove that each new term lies strictly between the preceding two terms. Suppose \(k\) is even and
\[
a_{k-1}<a_k<a_{k-2}.
\]
The decimal bases satisfy \(c_{k-1}<c_{k+1}<c_k\). Comparing both bases and exponents gives
\[
c_{k-1}^{a_{k-2}}
<c_{k+1}^{a_k}
<c_k^{a_{k-1}},
\]
which is exactly \(a_{k-1}<a_{k+1}<a_k\).

When \(k\ge3\) is odd, the corresponding assumptions are \(a_{k-2}<a_k<a_{k-1}\) and \(c_k<c_{k+1}<c_{k-1}\). They give
\[
c_k^{a_{k-1}}
<c_{k+1}^{a_k}
<c_{k-1}^{a_{k-2}},
\]
so \(a_k<a_{k+1}<a_{k-1}\). Starting with \(a_1<a_2<a_0\), these two steps apply alternately and prove the nesting for the entire sequence.

It follows that the odd-indexed terms strictly increase, the even-indexed terms strictly decrease, and the last odd term is below the last even term. Thus the decreasing order is
\[
a_2>a_4>\cdots>a_{2010}
>a_{2011}>a_{2009}>\cdots>a_1.
\]
All terms are distinct. There are \(1005\) even-indexed terms, so
\[
b_k=a_{2k}\qquad(1\le k\le1005).
\]
Equality \(a_k=b_k\) here would require \(k=2k\), impossible for positive \(k\).

For the remaining positions,
\[
b_k=a_{4023-2k}
\qquad(1006\le k\le2011).
\]
Distinctness now makes \(a_k=b_k\) equivalent to
\[
k=4023-2k,
\qquad k=1341.
\]
This lies in the required range and is the only matching index. The requested sum is therefore \(\boxed{1341}\), choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
